You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would. Once evidence in a session supports authorization for a next step or action, you should continue work without ending the turn to clarify with the user.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless given explicit instructions to do so, or instructed to do so as part of an explicitly-invoked skill or plugin. If authorized by a skill or plugin, name and link the skill or plugin in the final channel.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason. Put this explanation in a short, separate paragraph at the end of both commentary and final, after any permission question.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

When the user's prompt indicates a request for action, such as "can you...", "I want to...", "help me..." and similar expressions, treat these as instructions to do the work and take action. Do not stop at acknowledging capability (e.g. "Yes…"), proposing a plan, or offering to continue. Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment. 

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a lucid communicator. You speak warmly and candidly, as to someone you respect, and keep your own judgment. You disagree when you have reason; reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

Your writing adapts to the conversation, matching the tone and understanding of the user. Make sure to state the main point clearly and early, then develop it with the explanation and detail the reader needs. Let each sentence build on what came before. Develop the points that matter and provide enough support to be useful. 

Use plain, simple language: familiar words, concrete examples, and precise verbs. Prefer active voice and direct statements. Write in connected prose. Avoid section headings, and do not use concluding summary statements such as "In short:..", "The simplest mental model is:...".

Include technical details only when they help explain or substantiate the point; avoid scattering implementation details through the prose. Connect an action with its purpose, or a finding with its implication, rather than presenting them as separate fragments.

Default to using clear, concise paragraphs, each developing one main idea. Use lists only when the information is genuinely parallel, sequential, or easier to compare, and avoid nested lists unless the hierarchy cannot be expressed clearly in prose. 

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer." or "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely" or hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives. 

State the intended action directly. Avoid adding what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

## Technical communication

In addition to the writing style instructions above, follow these guidelines when discussing technical work: Use plain language over jargon, and reference technical details only to the degree that it actually helps with the conversation. Communicate complex concepts in a clear and cohesive manner. Translating complex topics into clear communication comes easy for you, and the user should never have to read your writing twice to understand it.

Lead with the outcome and then develop your reasoning for how you got there. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits. 

Present reasoning and evidence in the order that makes the conclusion easiest to assess, rather than recounting your work chronologically. Summarize routine verification instead of listing every check. In progress updates, focus on what you have learned, what remains uncertain, and what the next step will resolve.

### Writing PR descriptions

Lead the description with the concrete problem and resulting behavior. Use a concrete trigger and before/after example when helpful. Scale detail to complexity: simple PRs usually need one or two sentences plus relevant validation. Use structure when it helps scanning or the repository template requires it.

Describe the final change for a reviewer who has not seen the conversation. When scope changes, rewrite the title and description around the final implementation. Omit conversational history and abandoned approaches unless they explain a tradeoff needed for review. Include only technical and validation details that help reviewers assess the change.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

When available, you can use the `functions.request_user_input_async` tool to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. You can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Do NOT ask the user to upload files or send screenshots using this tool because the tool only supports text input. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 60 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermediate commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. 

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization. 

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead. 

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding. 

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.

- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.

- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.

- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not write tests for reversible, low-impact changes or that mirror the implementation. If you do choose to verify your work with tests, make sure that the tests are meaningful and necessary to verify implementation.
- Run tests appropriate to the change and complete required checks. Once those pass, broaden or repeat testing only when new changes, failures, or unresolved concerns justify it; otherwise, continue toward completing the task.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions. 

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name and link to the exact SKILL.md you read, quote the relevant instruction, and briefly explain how it applies. Distinguish explicit skill requirements from your interpretation. If a skill does not explicitly require approval, default to proceeding within the user’s authorized scope rather than asking for confirmation based on an inferred requirement.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and orchestrator skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"orchestrator"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible. 

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Apps (Connectors)

Apps (Connectors) can be explicitly triggered in user messages in the format `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. Apps can also be implicitly triggered as long as the context suggests usage of available apps.
An app is equivalent to a set of MCP tools within the `codex_apps` MCP.
An installed app's MCP tools are either provided to you already, or can be lazy-loaded through the `tool_search` tool. If `tool_search` is available, the apps that are searchable by `tools_search` will be listed by it.
Do not additionally call list_mcp_resources or list_mcp_resource_templates for apps.

# Plugins

A plugin is a local bundle of skills, MCP servers, and apps.

## How to use plugins

- Skill naming: If a plugin contributes skills, those skill entries are prefixed with plugin_name: in the Skills list.
- MCP naming: Plugin-provided MCP tools keep standard MCP identifiers such as mcp__server__tool; use tool provenance to tell which plugin they come from.
- Trigger rules: If the user explicitly names a plugin, prefer capabilities associated with that plugin for that turn.
- Relationship to capabilities: Plugins are not invoked directly. Use their underlying skills, MCP tools, and app tools to help solve the task.
- Relevance: Determine what a plugin can help with from explicit user mention or from the plugin-associated skills, MCP tools, and apps exposed elsewhere in this turn.
- Missing/blocked: If the user requests a plugin that does not have relevant callable capabilities for the task, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions. 

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name and link to the exact SKILL.md you read, quote the relevant instruction, and briefly explain how it applies. Distinguish explicit skill requirements from your interpretation. If a skill does not explicitly require approval, default to proceeding within the user’s authorized scope rather than asking for confirmation based on an inferred requirement.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and orchestrator skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"orchestrator"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible. 

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Apps (Connectors)

Apps (Connectors) can be explicitly triggered in user messages in the format `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. Apps can also be implicitly triggered as long as the context suggests usage of available apps.
An app is equivalent to a set of MCP tools within the `codex_apps` MCP.
An installed app's MCP tools are either provided to you already, or can be lazy-loaded through the `tool_search` tool. If `tool_search` is available, the apps that are searchable by `tools_search` will be listed by it.
Do not additionally call list_mcp_resources or list_mcp_resource_templates for apps.

# Plugins

A plugin is a local bundle of skills, MCP servers, and apps.

## How to use plugins

- Skill naming: If a plugin contributes skills, those skill entries are prefixed with plugin_name: in the Skills list.
- MCP naming: Plugin-provided MCP tools keep standard MCP identifiers such as mcp__server__tool; use tool provenance to tell which plugin they come from.
- Trigger rules: If the user explicitly names a plugin, prefer capabilities associated with that plugin for that turn.

content.text: why do we need a dispatch queue?

**The queue holds accepted tasks until a worker can run them.** We don’t necessarily need a separate queue service.

Example: both browser workers are busy when a third Slack request arrives. We save that request, acknowledge it, and run it when capacity becomes available.

In this draft, it serves three purposes:

1. **Handle busy workers:** pending requests wait without blocking Slack intake.
2. **Survive restarts:** accepted tasks remain recorded. Safe resumption also needs saved progress.
3. **Control concurrency:** limit active tasks and prevent conflicting runs from changing the same browser or profile.

For v1, **a durable task table plus dispatch logic could fill that box**. A dedicated queue is an implementation choice we haven’t justified yet.

content.text: yeah we would need a task queue there fs because we are gonna spin up a VM box in realtime or something like that and its possible that start/resuming a VM would fail. so we dont want to lose the task there. so queue is a great choice. my next question is how man failures could we sustain in this way? we don't have infinite resources do we?

**We choose a failure budget.** The queue preserves pending work; it doesn’t give us unlimited retries or storage.

An initial policy could be:

1. **Per task:** allow **3 VM start/resume attempts within 10 minutes**, whichever limit comes first. Space retries out; stop immediately for permanent errors like invalid configuration.
2. **During a provider outage:** pause normal dispatch and make occasional recovery checks. Retrying every queued task would amplify the outage. [Retry guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/retry).
3. **Across the system:** cap pending tasks, simultaneous VM starts, running VMs, and runtime/spend. When admission capacity is full, clearly reject new work.
4. **After exhausting retries:** mark the task failed, notify its owner, and stop spending compute on it. Retain its failure record for a bounded period so it can be inspected or explicitly retried. That’s the role of a [dead-letter queue](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html).

For capacity, **100 free queue slots receiving 10 tasks/minute buys roughly 10 minutes of outage buffer**, assuming nothing completes or expires.

One crucial VM detail: **a launch timeout might mean the VM started but its response was lost.** We must reconcile provider state and use supported idempotency before launching another, or retries could create duplicate billable VMs.

The **3-attempt/10-minute limit is a starting proposal**. We’d tune it against measured startup times and our actual hosting budget.

content.text: what does the fair dispatch leases means in there?

They’re two separate things:

1. **Fair dispatch = whose task runs next.**  
   If workspace A submits 100 tasks and workspace B submits one, B should get a turn without waiting behind all 100. The scheduler shares available workers according to quotas.

2. **Lease = a temporary claim on a task.**  
   A worker claims: “I’m handling task 123 for the next 60 seconds.” It periodically renews that claim while working. If it crashes and stops renewing, the lease expires and another worker can take over. **60 seconds is just an example.**

The important catch: an expired worker might still be alive but disconnected. We must reject its further updates or actions after takeover, so two workers don’t execute the same task.

**Fair dispatch prevents starvation. Leases let us recover work when a worker disappears.**

---
name: i-have-adhd
description: Use whenever responding to a user with ADHD or requesting ADHD-friendly communication, including technical work, explanations, planning, task initiation, and casual conversation, even without explicitly asking for brevity or structure.
---

# ADHD-Friendly Responses

Shape responses so the reader can act without retaining context.

## Response contract

1. For a task, make the first sentence an imperative, sub-two-minute action; put no reassurance or context before it. For a question, give the direct answer. Never announce this skill.
2. Number multi-step work: one action per step, five items per visible list. Shape plans as `Now` (up to five actions plus a done condition), `Later` (one line of phase names), `State`, and `Next`. Expand nothing else.
3. Restate the current step and progress. Surface wins, defer tangents, and use concrete time estimates.
4. For errors, state failure, evidence or cause, and fix. After three failed attempts, name the suspect assumption and ask one diagnostic question.
5. End unfinished work with one imperative, sub-two-minute action and nothing after it. If complete, end with the verified outcome.

## Exceptions

- Explain fully when asked, using skimmable headings.
- Confirm destructive or irreversible actions.
- Ask one question for material ambiguity.
- Let safety, accuracy, and explicit instructions override brevity.

## Pre-send check

Remove announcements, closing pleasantries, tangents, empty hedging, and buried wins. Ensure the first and last lines carry the action or outcome.

verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:15:- Traced Slack identity, route selection, turn scope, agent tool dispatch, memory, recall, terminal/files/code, browser/vault state, result delivery and owner approval. Independent reviews are linked below.

verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:26:| Browser and saved account access | Vault authority is profile-scoped. Several browser persistence/naming modes intentionally share state within a profile; the real-profile CDP cache also has a process-global slot. | Source and bounded dummy vault/cache probes | Separate owner/audience profiles; choose and verify browser/backend persistence deliberately; constrain selectable sessions and avoid shared real-profile attachment. |
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:27:| Arbitrary execution and publication | Local execution has the server account's permissions. Docker can contain terminal/files/code but does not automatically constrain every host-side tool or copied transcript. Native outbound messaging and shared approval cards do not supply owner-approved publication semantics. | Source; local execution/approval probes in supporting reports | Actual execution isolation plus constrained host tools, protected shared stores, and an owner/content/audience-bound publishing path. |
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:96:## 4. Account/browser authority follows profiles and backend semantics
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:98:The pinned release contains the credential vault; these findings do not rely on vault code from a newer commit. Vault entries and external-vault unlock tokens are scoped to the Hermes home, not separately to each Slack sender. A browser task ID does not add an owner field to a vault entry. Origin checks prevent filling credentials on the wrong website; they do not decide which human may use a saved login for the correct website.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:100:The browser/vault review reproduced a second session in the same profile listing a dummy login, reusing a dummy external-vault unlock token, and reaching the fill boundary with that login. Browser socket interaction was replaced with a fake. Separate profile homes gave separate normal vault/token visibility.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:102:Browser identity is backend-specific. Named Browser Use sessions can override per-task separation within a profile; persistent Camofox identity is shared within a profile by design. Real-profile attachment uses a process-global CDP cache; a dummy cache probe demonstrated reuse across home scopes. This last observation is a cache-level reproduction, not evidence of an actual cross-user browser session having been driven.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:104:There is also an execution distinction: `browser_exec` runs Python through a **host subprocess**, even if that Python controls a remote browser. `model_tools.py:391-395` explicitly documents host execution and hides this tool when terminal capability is absent; `tools/browser_use_cli.py:594-600,612-662` launches it directly. Selecting Docker for the terminal does not reroute this separate launch into that Docker environment. Keeping this path enabled requires isolating its host execution or changing the execution path; an alternative is a constrained browser tool/backend that preserves the required browser workflow. This is source evidence, not a live Browser Use execution test.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:106:Detailed source references, controls and bounded reproduction evidence are in the [browser/vault audit](audit-browser-notes.md).
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:116:Private final replies are copied into the launch home's delivery ledger for recovery (`gateway/delivery_ledger.py:171-184,270-283`). That is not itself an end-user leak. It means a worker must not have unrestricted access to this shared store, even if each profile's primary session database is separate.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:118:For publication, native Slack `send_message` accepts a model-selected destination without an owner/content/audience approval record. Shared Slack approval buttons check whether the clicker may use the bot, not whether they own the private action. A dummy handler probe allowed another admitted user to reach the resolver. Private DM controls restrict visibility, but stock shared cards do not establish the required ownership check.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:124:1. **Reject a single shared profile for reviewers' private accounts and shared context.** Independent chat sessions are not enough for profile-scoped memory, vault and browser persistence.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:126:3. **Constrain every cross-context access path.** Disable unrestricted recall or replace it with enforced scoped recall; choose an isolated browser backend; constrain arbitrary execution and host-side tools. Disabling a feature is acceptable only if the required product experience still works.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:127:4. **Provide owner-bound private work and publication.** If a shared task needs private account work, keep its observations private and release only approved content to an approved audience. Stock general-purpose outbound tools/shared approval cards do not prove this flow.
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:132:**Configuration-only remains a candidate for a restricted tool set.** Separate audience profiles, private Docker mounts, unrestricted recall disabled, no host Python browser path or shared authenticated CDP endpoint, inline skill shell off, and constrained outbound tools can remove the demonstrated paths. This audit does not prove that every such stock configuration fails. It also does not verify one that preserves every v1 feature. Automated private-to-shared publication still needs enforceable owner/content/audience mediation; a manual workflow must not silently replace required behavior.

verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:142:| Vault/browser probe | 12 observations matched | Dummy vaults/tokens and mocked browser/cache boundaries; [source](probes/browser_vault_ownership.py), [observations](evidence/browser_vault_ownership.json). |
verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:149:Live Slack/model/browser behavior, concurrent authenticated tasks, browser backend deployment, real access lifecycle and hosted restart recovery remain unverified. No source audit can establish that a model will never select a dangerous tool argument. Here, the acceptance concern is already decidable: the required forbidden access is currently available through an enabled stock capability. Fixing or removing that capability does not require waiting for an accidental leak.

verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:98:The pinned release contains the credential vault; these findings do not rely on vault code from a newer commit. verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:100:The browser/vault review reproduced a second session in the same profile listing a dummy login, reusing a dummy external-vault unlock token, and reaching the fill boundary with that login. verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:102:Browser identity is backend-specific. verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:106:Detailed source references, controls and bounded reproduction evidence are in the [browser/vault audit](audit-browser-notes.md).

name: i-have-adhd
description: Use whenever responding to a user with ADHD or requesting ADHD-friendly communication, including technical work, explanations, planning, task initiation, and casual conversation, even without explicitly asking for brevity or structure.

# ADHD-Friendly Responses

Shape responses so the reader can act without retaining context.

## Response contract

1. For a task, make the first sentence an imperative, sub-two-minute action; put no reassurance or context before it. For a question, give the direct answer. Never announce this skill.
2. Number multi-step work: one action per step, five items per visible list. Shape plans as `Now` (up to five actions plus a done condition), `Later` (one line of phase names), `State`, and `Next`. Expand nothing else.
3. Restate the current step and progress. Surface wins, defer tangents, and use concrete time estimates.
4. For errors, state failure, evidence or cause, and fix. After three failed attempts, name the suspect assumption and ask one diagnostic question.
5. End unfinished work with one imperative, sub-two-minute action and nothing after it. If complete, end with the verified outcome.

## Exceptions

- Explain fully when asked, using skimmable headings.
- Confirm destructive or irreversible actions.
- Ask one question for material ambiguity.
- Let safety, accuracy, and explicit instructions override brevity.

## Pre-send check

Remove announcements, closing pleasantries, tangents, empty hedging, and buried wins. Ensure the first and last lines carry the action or outcome.

item.stdout:
## 5. Execution isolation and sharing need explicit enforcement

Profiles are not OS sandboxes. The default local terminal executes with the host account's permissions, as both the [official documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/#profiles-vs-workspaces-vs-sandboxing) and source describe.

An important qualification: the pinned file tools and `execute_code` do follow the selected remote terminal backend. It would be incorrect to say they always run on the host even after Docker is selected. Docker can therefore close a substantial part of the file/code boundary if its mounts, users and lifecycle are appropriate. Persistent Docker defaults to one container per profile, shared by that profile's sessions, so the profile mapping still matters.

Other handlers, including recall and memory, execute in the Hermes host process. A terminal container alone does not constrain the cross-profile database read reproduced above. A full runtime container with all users' data mounted together would also retain the problem. Every accessible store and tool must follow the chosen trust boundary.

Private final replies are copied into the launch home's delivery ledger for recovery (`gateway/delivery_ledger.py:171-184,270-283`). That is not itself an end-user leak. It means a worker must not have unrestricted access to this shared store, even if each profile's primary session database is separate.

For publication, native Slack `send_message` accepts a model-selected destination without an owner/content/audience approval record. Shared Slack approval buttons check whether the clicker may use the bot, not whether they own the private action. A dummy handler probe allowed another admitted user to reach the resolver. Private DM controls restrict visibility, but stock shared cards do not establish the required ownership check.

Detailed paths and probe limits: [execution audit](audit-execution-notes.md), [Slack audit](audit-slack-notes.md).

## What this establishes for the design

1. **Reject a single shared profile for reviewers' private accounts and shared context.** Independent chat sessions are not enough for profile-scoped memory, vault and browser persistence.
2. **Use explicit private and audience profile routing.** Keep unknown routes unprivileged and verify tenant admission. This reuses existing Hermes machinery.
3. **Constrain every cross-context access path.** Disable unrestricted recall or replace it with enforced scoped recall; choose an isolated browser backend; constrain arbitrary execution and host-side tools. Disabling a feature is acceptable only if the required product experience still works.
4. **Provide owner-bound private work and publication.** If a shared task needs private account work, keep its observations private and release only approved content to an approved audience. Stock general-purpose outbound tools/shared approval cards do not prove this flow.
5. **Select the smallest enforceable deployment after checking the active tool inventory.** A shared trusted gateway plus correctly isolated tools may suffice. Separate whole runtimes are an alternative if host-side access cannot be constrained reliably. The evidence does not mandate a permanent instance per person.

Plugin hooks are a possible implementation seam, not automatic proof of enforcement. The actual pre-tool callback dispatcher blocks callback errors/timeouts; some outer error handling and the gateway-dispatch hook are fail-open. A policy must have reliable identity, complete path coverage and defined failure behavior. Inspecting shell strings is not a substitute for execution isolation.

**Configuration-only remains a candidate for a restricted tool set.** Separate audience profiles, private Docker mounts, unrestricted recall disabled, no host Python browser path or shared authenticated CDP endpoint, inline skill shell off, and constrained outbound tools can remove the demonstrated paths. This audit does not prove that every such stock configuration fails. It also does not verify one that preserves every v1 feature. Automated private-to-shared publication still needs enforceable owner/content/audience mediation; a manual workflow must not silently replace required behavior.

## Recorded checks

| Check | Result | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seven selected routing/identity/approval/delivery test files | 40 upstream tests passed | Synthetic upstream fixtures; see [captured output](evidence/2026-10-03-slack-audit-tests.txt). |
| Upstream named-profile recall test | 1 passed | Confirms upstream intentionally supports cross-profile recall. |
| Local memory/recall probes | 6 passed as behavior witnesses | Four exposure cases and two positive controls; not privacy acceptance. |
| Slack route/approval/MPIM probe | Expected findings reproduced | Fake transport/resolver; [source](probes/slack_boundary_probe.py), [observations](evidence/2026-10-03-slack-boundary-probe.json). |
| Vault/browser probe | 12 observations matched | Dummy vaults/tokens and mocked browser/cache boundaries; [source](probes/browser_vault_ownership.py), [observations](evidence/browser_vault_ownership.json). |
| Filesystem/dispatch/policy probe | Read and policy behaviors reproduced | Dummy files, real dispatch and callback handling; see [execution report](audit-execution-notes.md). |

The upstream tracked checkout remained unchanged. Only research notes, probe sources and sanitized evidence were added to clanker's repository.

## Remaining uncertainty

Live Slack/model/browser behavior, concurrent authenticated tasks, browser backend deployment, real access lifecycle and hosted restart recovery remain unverified. No source audit can establish that a model will never select a dangerous tool argument. Here, the acceptance concern is already decidable: the required forbidden access is currently available through an enabled stock capability. Fixing or removing that capability does not require waiting for an accidental leak.

The next engineering decision is which active tools and shared/private deployment boundary to retain. This report does not change `V1_SCOPE.md`, adopt a new architecture, or implement any fixes.

This needs a focused test for another admitted user, an old card and changed action details. Hermes documents immediate `/bg` acknowledgement, progress, cancellation, session persistence and a durable final-response delivery ledger. These are reusable primitives. Profiles are not OS sandboxes. The default local terminal executes with the host account's permissions, as both the [official documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/#profiles-vs-workspaces-vs-sandboxing) and source describe.

An important qualification: the pinned file tools and `execute_code` do follow the selected remote terminal backend. It would be incorrect to say they always run on the host even after Docker is selected. Docker can therefore close a substantial part of the file/code boundary if its mounts, users and lifecycle are appropriate. Persistent Docker defaults to one container per profile, shared by that profile's sessions, so the profile mapping still matters.

Other handlers, including recall and memory, execute in the Hermes host process. A terminal container alone does not constrain the cross-profile database read reproduced above. A full runtime container with all users' data mounted together would also retain the problem. Every accessible store and tool must follow the chosen trust boundary.

Private final replies are copied into the launch home's delivery ledger for recovery (`gateway/delivery_ledger.py:171-184,270-283`). That is not itself an end-user leak. It means a worker must not have unrestricted access to this shared store, even if each profile's primary session database is separate.

For publication, native Slack `send_message` accepts a model-selected destination without an owner/content/audience approval record. Shared Slack approval buttons check whether the clicker may use the bot, not whether they own the private action. A dummy handler probe allowed another admitted user to reach the resolver. Private DM controls restrict visibility, but stock shared cards do not establish the required ownership check.

Detailed paths and probe limits: [execution audit](audit-execution-notes.md), [Slack audit](audit-slack-notes.md).

## What this establishes for the design

1. **Reject a single shared profile for reviewers' private accounts and shared context.** Independent chat sessions are not enough for profile-scoped memory, vault and browser persistence.
2. **Use explicit private and audience profile routing.** Keep unknown routes unprivileged and verify tenant admission. This reuses existing Hermes machinery.
3. **Constrain every cross-context access path.** Disable unrestricted recall or replace it with enforced scoped recall; choose an isolated browser backend; constrain arbitrary execution and host-side tools. Disabling a feature is acceptable only if the required product experience still works.
4. **Provide owner-bound private work and publication.** If a shared task needs private account work, keep its observations private and release only approved content to an approved audience. Stock general-purpose outbound tools/shared approval cards do not prove this flow.
5. **Select the smallest enforceable deployment after checking the active tool inventory.** A shared trusted gateway plus correctly isolated tools may suffice. Separate whole runtimes are an alternative if host-side access cannot be constrained reliably. The evidence does not mandate a permanent instance per person.

Plugin hooks are a possible implementation seam, not automatic proof of enforcement. The actual pre-tool callback dispatcher blocks callback errors/timeouts; some outer error handling and the gateway-dispatch hook are fail-open. A policy must have reliable identity, complete path coverage and defined failure behavior. Inspecting shell strings is not a substitute for execution isolation.

**Configuration-only remains a candidate for a restricted tool set.** Separate audience profiles, private Docker mounts, unrestricted recall disabled, no host Python browser path or shared authenticated CDP endpoint, inline skill shell off, and constrained outbound tools can remove the demonstrated paths. This audit does not prove that every such stock configuration fails. It also does not verify one that preserves every v1 feature. Automated private-to-shared publication still needs enforceable owner/content/audience mediation; a manual workflow must not silently replace required behavior.

- **Hermes supplies useful recovery primitives, but Clanker’s hosted recovery is unverified.** The review records `/bg`, progress, cancellation, session persistence, and a durable **final-response delivery ledger**. Those do not establish a durable distributed browser-task workflow. See [recovery review](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/HERMES_VERIFICATION_REVIEW.md:61) and [remaining uncertainty](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:147).
- **Lease renewal needs a worker supervisor independent of model/tool progress.** A lengthy browser call must not expire the task’s claim. The inspected reports provide no evidence of Clanker’s VM lease heartbeat or fencing implementation. Lease expiry must prevent stale execution before another worker takes over; a heartbeat alone cannot stop duplicate website actions.
- **“No recent activity” must not mean “safe to stop.”** The autoscaler should protect allocated/running VMs, including slow browser calls, and apply idle timeout only after an explicit release or safe transition. Separately enforce total runtime/spend limits: the review explicitly notes that inactivity timeout is not total task duration. [Runtime limits finding](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/HERMES_VERIFICATION_REVIEW.md:69).
- **Waiting for the user needs durable task state.** Proposed integration: save `waiting_for_input`/`waiting_for_approval`, bind the response to the owner, task, exact action and expiry, then resume that task. Release or suspend its VM only when the selected backend can safely preserve/reconstruct the needed state; otherwise keep it reserved under a bounded timeout. Missing-input resumption remains untested, and stock shared approval cards failed the owner check in a dummy probe. [Approval audit](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md:118).
- **Recovery must reconcile external actions before retrying.** If a website accepted a submission before the VM died, a queue retry can duplicate it. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# Invoke the pinned stock Hermes checkout with dedicated local state.
# This is not a security sandbox; use dummy data for boundary experiments.
set -euo pipefail
umask 077

project_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
lab_dir="$project_dir/.local/hermes-lab"

if [[ ! -x "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" ]]; then
  echo "Install the pinned baseline first; see verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ -e "$lab_dir/upstream/.env" ]]; then
  echo "The upstream checkout has a fallback .env; keep credentials only in the lab home." >&2
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$lab_dir/home" "$lab_dir/workspace" "$lab_dir/gateway-locks" "$lab_dir/managed"
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml" ]]; then
  cp "$project_dir/verification/hermes/config.yaml" "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml"
fi
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/.env" ]]; then
  touch "$lab_dir/home/.env"
fi
chmod 600 "$lab_dir/home/.env"

cd "$lab_dir/workspace"
# Credentials must be deliberately configured in the lab home. Keep HOME
# unchanged for platform compatibility; do not inherit provider/session vars.
# Command smoke: skip startup model/tool warmup until inference is configured.
exec env -i \
  HOME="$HOME" \
  PATH="$lab_dir/venv/bin:$PATH" \
  TERM="${TERM:-xterm-256color}" \
  LANG="${LANG:-en_US.UTF-8}" \
  HERMES_HOME="$lab_dir/home" \
  HERMES_MANAGED_DIR="$lab_dir/managed" \
  HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR="$lab_dir/gateway-locks" \
  HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1 \
  HERMES_STARTUP_WARMUP_TIMEOUT=0 \
  "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" "$@"

     2	WAL, owner pid + process-start liveness, bounded retention) so a crash between finalize and
     3	platform ACK cannot lose a response silently. Checkpoints: record_obligation() 'pending' before
     4	any send | mark_attempting() 'attempting' right before the await | mark_delivered() 'delivered'
     5	only on SendResult.success | mark_failed() 'failed' on a definitive rejection. Crash semantics
     6	(never silently resend an ambiguous send): pending = never started, redeliver plainly; attempting
     7	= crashed mid-await, platform MAY have it, redeliver WITH a visible recovered marker; failed =
     8	rejected once, restart is a retry boundary, also marked; delivered = prune. Attempts are capped
     9	and stale rows expire, both -> 'abandoned' (kept briefly, then pruned). Everything is
    10	best-effort: ledger failures must never block a send; callers wrap every call in try/except.

**Yes: the existing Hermes gateway automatically sends a returned answer to Slack.** Verified at pinned commit `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`.

- **Actual send chain:** [`base.py:4455`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/platforms/base.py:4455) awaits the message handler; nonempty text reaches `_send_final_text` at **4506–4509** → `send_final_ledgered` at **4289** → `_send_with_retry` at **4272** → adapter `send()`. [`slack/adapter.py:2241`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:2241) resolves the reply thread, and **2290–2292** calls `chat_postMessage` with the workspace-specific client. An existing native stream is finalized instead of posting twice (**2227–2231**).
- **The gateway already records outgoing final text before sending.** [`base.py:4121`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/platforms/base.py:4121) records destination, thread and content; **4166–4170** marks delivery success/failure. It skips slash-command/ephemeral replies, can be disabled, and ledger writes are best-effort. [`delivery_ledger.py:1`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/delivery_ledger.py:1) documents bounded retry and visible duplicate warnings after ambiguous sends.
- **Turn ending does not always produce a new final post.** Empty/streamed/queued responses are skipped; an interrupted response with a pending replacement is suppressed at [`base.py:4464`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/platforms/base.py:4464). `CancelledError` is re-raised at **4533–4538**. Other exceptions invoke a best-effort error notice via **4542** and **4296–4313**.
- **Proposed remote-VM split still needs a result bridge.** Keeping the Slack gateway alive preserves its existing delivery machinery, but launching standalone Hermes on another VM does not itself return its output into that gateway’s waiting message handler. We need authenticated task/result correlation and durable result handoff before stopping the VM, then invoke/reuse this delivery path. **We do not need to rewrite Slack posting; we do need the worker-to-gateway integration.**

- **Native Hermes selects a profile per incoming message.** Routing matches configured platform, bot, user, chat and thread criteria; the most specific match wins. `session_identity.py` stamps `source.profile` and resolves `runtime_home`, separately retaining the transport bot’s authorization home. - **It activates that profile through request-local context, not a global profile switch.** The gateway wraps message handling in `_async_profile_runtime_scope`; this sets context-local home, credential and terminal scopes, then restores them. `get_hermes_home()` consults that override first. 8:# Browser Automation
12:- **Browser Use cloud mode** via [Browser Use](https://browser-use.com) for managed Chromium with stealth, residential proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and reusable browser profiles
14:- **Browser Use mode** via the [Browser Use CLI 3.0](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use), the default browser driver for local Chrome and Browser Use cloud browsers
16:- **Camofox local mode** via [Camofox](https://github.com/jo-inc/camofox-browser) for local anti-detection browsing (Firefox-based fingerprint spoofing)
17:- **Lightpanda local engine** via [Lightpanda](https://lightpanda.io) — a headless browser built from scratch in Zig for machines; instant start up, 16x lower memory and 9x faster than Chrome. Works in Browser Use mode (Hermes spawns it, no Chromium or Node needed) and with the built-in tools (automatic Chrome fallback for actions it doesn't support yet)
19:- **Local browser mode** via the `agent-browser` CLI and a local Chromium installation
23:## Overview
32:- **Persistent cloud profiles** — Browser Use Cloud can reuse cookies, localStorage, and saved passwords across sessions
37:## Setup
40:If you have a paid [Nous Portal](https://portal.nousresearch.com) subscription, you can use browser automation through the **[Tool Gateway](tool-gateway.md)** without any separate API keys. New installs can run `hermes setup --portal` to log in and turn on every gateway tool at once; existing installs can pick **Nous Subscription** as the browser provider via `hermes model` or `hermes tools`.
43:### Browser Use cloud mode
48:# Add to ~/.hermes/.env
52:Get your API key at [browser-use.com](https://browser-use.com).
54:Browser Use Cloud runs managed Chromium with [stealth](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/browser/stealth) and [residential proxies](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/browser/proxies) enabled by default, includes CAPTCHA solving, and supports [persistent profiles](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/guides/authentication) for cookies, localStorage, and saved passwords.
56:### Browserbase cloud mode
61:# Add to ~/.hermes/.env
66:Get your credentials at [browserbase.com](https://browserbase.com).
69:The `.env` keys above supply **credentials only**. The active cloud browser is chosen by the `browser.cloud_provider` selection written by `hermes tools` → Browser Automation (`browserbase`, `browser-use`, `camofox`, or `nous` for the Nous Subscription). Once a selection exists, adding or removing a key does not switch providers — and a selected provider with a missing key errors with guidance to run `hermes tools` instead of silently rerouting. Never-configured setups still autodetect from available credentials.
72:### Browser Use mode (default)
74:Browser Use mode uses the [Browser Use CLI 3.0](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use) instead of the built-in browser tools. The agent writes and executes Python in the browser to click, type, drag, scrape, and interact with webpages.
76:**This is the default browser mode**: when `browser.backend` is unset and the `browser-use` CLI is runnable (installed, or available through `uvx`), the agent gets the single `browser_exec` tool. If the CLI can't run, Hermes falls back to the built-in browser tools automatically.
78:The mode is a **driver** that composes with your configured browser backend: it drives Hermes' own headless Chromium, a Nous-subscription cloud browser, Browserbase, Firecrawl, or Browser Use cloud browsers — whichever browser source is selected in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation. The one exception is Camofox, which has no CDP endpoint for the harness to attach to; Camofox setups automatically keep the built-in browser tools.
80:**Local browsing uses the packaged Chromium, not your own Chrome.** With no cloud provider or `/browser connect` endpoint configured, Hermes launches the same Chromium that the built-in tools use (installed via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, driven through agent-browser) and points the Browser Use CLI at it. Your installed Chrome is never touched, so there is no `chrome://inspect` remote-debugging toggle to enable and no "Allow remote debugging?" popup — and it works on headless hosts with no Chrome at all. The browser is shared with the built-in stack's lifecycle: it is closed after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, at exit, and by the orphan sweep. To drive a browser you're signed in to, use `/browser connect` or the [real-profile toggle](#real-profile-browsing-use-your-own-logins).

89:  backend: "off"
92:(`backend: "browser-use"` remains valid to force the mode explicitly.)

Install the binary and put it on your `PATH` (see the [Lightpanda installation guide](https://lightpanda.io/docs/run-locally/installation/one-liner)), then pick **Lightpanda** in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, or set:

508:- **Browser Use mode (the default).** Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself — one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task) — and points the Browser Use CLI at it. No Chromium, Playwright or Node.js is needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. All of these processes share one on-disk HTTP cache at `$HERMES_HOME/cache/browser-use/lightpanda/http-cache`, so repeat visits skip re-downloading assets. Hermes passes the cache flag only when the installed Lightpanda supports it (0.3.x+); older binaries simply run without a cache. To clear it, stop your Lightpanda sessions first, then delete that directory. Lightpanda has no graphical renderer, so `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable and the tool description tells the model to work text-first; it also holds one page per session, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (tracked upstream in [lightpanda-io/browser#1962](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/issues/1962)).
509:- **Built-in browser tools** (`/browser use off`). Hermes drives Lightpanda through `agent-browser --engine lightpanda` over CDP, the same way it drives local Chrome, with **automatic Chrome fallback**: Lightpanda handles the actions it supports (navigate, snapshot, click, type, scroll, back, press, eval) and Hermes transparently retries on Chrome for anything it doesn't. Screenshots and `browser_vision` are routed straight to Chrome.

513:### Local Chromium-family browser via CDP (`/browser connect`)
530:If a browser isn't already running with remote debugging, Hermes will attempt to auto-launch a supported Chromium-family browser with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. Detection includes Brave, Brave Origin/Nightly, Google Chrome, Chromium, and Microsoft Edge, with common Linux install paths and binary names such as `brave-origin`, `brave-origin-nightly`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin-nightly/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave-bin/brave`, and `/snap/bin/brave`.
533:To start a Chromium-family browser manually with CDP enabled, use a dedicated user-data-dir so the debug port actually comes up even if the browser is already running with your normal profile:
536:# Linux — Brave
543:# Linux — Google Chrome
550:# macOS — Brave
557:# macOS — Google Chrome
567:**Why `--user-data-dir`?** Without it, launching a Chromium-family browser while a regular instance is already running typically opens a new window on the existing process — and that existing process was not started with `--remote-debugging-port`, so port 9222 never opens. A dedicated user-data-dir forces a fresh browser process where the debug port actually listens. `--no-first-run --no-default-browser-check` skips the first-launch wizard for the fresh profile.
569:**Chrome 136+ makes the dedicated profile mandatory.** Two separate mechanisms are in play, and neither applies once you pass a non-default `--user-data-dir`. First, since [Chrome 136](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port) `--remote-debugging-port` and `--remote-debugging-pipe` "will no longer be respected if attempting to debug the default Chrome data directory" — the flag is silently ignored, no dialog, and `/browser connect` (or `curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`) gets connection refused even from a cold start. Second, [Chrome 144+](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp-debug-your-browser-session) adds an opt-in *approval* flow for debugging your real profile: you enable it under `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`, and Chrome then shows an **"Allow remote debugging?"** dialog for **every incoming connection** (not once per launch), with nothing listening until you press **Allow**. If you see that dialog, you are on the approval path, not the flag path. The fix is exactly the commands above: point `--user-data-dir` somewhere other than your default profile directory (e.g. `$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug`), which needs neither the toggle nor the dialog. This applies to Chrome, Chromium, Edge, and Brave builds that have picked up the change.
571:A dedicated profile starts out signed out of everything. If you want the agent to browse with your existing logins *and* no approval dialog, use [`browser.use_real_profile`](#real-profile-browsing-use-your-own-logins) instead: it snapshots your active profile into a copy and drives that, which is a non-default user-data-dir and so never triggers either mechanism.

439:When another app drives the visible Camofox browser (a desktop assistant, a custom integration, another agent), configure Hermes to operate inside that same identity instead of spawning its own isolated profile.

467:- Hermes skips destructive cleanup at task end (same as `managed_persistence: true`). The other app's tab/cookies/profile survive.
477:Adoption only fires until `tab_id` is populated for the session. If the external app closes the adopted tab mid-run, the next browser tool call will surface a Camofox error — Hermes does not re-poll for a fresh tab on every call.
479:**Picking `session_key`:** if you want Hermes to reliably attach to a *specific* existing tab, set `session_key` to the `listItemId` the external app used when creating it. If you leave `session_key` unset and only set `user_id`, Hermes generates a per-task `session_key` (`task_<id>`) — Hermes will share cookies and the profile with the external app, but will open its own tab alongside instead of reusing one.
481:**Concurrency note:** the external app and Hermes can drive the same Camofox `userId` simultaneously, but Camofox does not coordinate per-tab focus between clients. Coordinate ownership at the application layer (e.g. the external app pauses while Hermes runs).

487:### Lightpanda local engine
489:[Lightpanda](https://lightpanda.io) is an open-source headless browser written from scratch. It starts instantly, runs 9x faster and uses 16x less memory than Chrome, which matters for agents that live on small VMs for long stretches.
491:Lightpanda is a **local engine** (a browser source, like "Local Browser"), not a cloud provider. Install the binary and put it on your `PATH` (see the [Lightpanda installation guide](https://lightpanda.io/docs/run-locally/installation/one-liner)), then pick **Lightpanda** in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, or set:
494:# Add to ~/.hermes/config.yaml
496:  cloud_provider: local
497:  engine: lightpanda
508:- **Browser Use mode (the default).** Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself — one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task) — and points the Browser Use CLI at it. No Chromium, Playwright or Node.js is needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. All of these processes share one on-disk HTTP cache at `$HERMES_HOME/cache/browser-use/lightpanda/http-cache`, so repeat visits skip re-downloading assets. Hermes passes the cache flag only when the installed Lightpanda supports it (0.3.x+); older binaries simply run without a cache. To clear it, stop your Lightpanda sessions first, then delete that directory. Lightpanda has no graphical renderer, so `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable and the tool description tells the model to work text-first; it also holds one page per session, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (tracked upstream in [lightpanda-io/browser#1962](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/issues/1962)).
509:- **Built-in browser tools** (`/browser use off`). Hermes drives Lightpanda through `agent-browser --engine lightpanda` over CDP, the same way it drives local Chrome, with **automatic Chrome fallback**: Lightpanda handles the actions it supports (navigate, snapshot, click, type, scroll, back, press, eval) and Hermes transparently retries on Chrome for anything it doesn't. Screenshots and `browser_vision` are routed straight to Chrome.
511:**When the engine is ignored.** `browser.engine` is the lowest-precedence browser setting: a cloud provider (including the Nous subscription browser — and on never-configured setups, any `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` / `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env` auto-selects one), Camofox, a `browser.cdp_url` / `/browser connect` override, or `browser.use_real_profile` all take precedence. Picking Lightpanda in `hermes tools` writes `cloud_provider: local` for you; `/browser status` and `hermes doctor` report when the engine is configured but shadowed, and by what.
513:### Local Chromium-family browser via CDP (`/browser connect`)
530:If a browser isn't already running with remote debugging, Hermes will attempt to auto-launch a supported Chromium-family browser with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. Detection includes Brave, Brave Origin/Nightly, Google Chrome, Chromium, and Microsoft Edge, with common Linux install paths and binary names such as `brave-origin`, `brave-origin-nightly`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave.com/brave-origin-nightly/brave-origin`, `/opt/brave-bin/brave`, and `/snap/bin/brave`.
533:To start a Chromium-family browser manually with CDP enabled, use a dedicated user-data-dir so the debug port actually comes up even if the browser is already running with your normal profile:
536:# Linux — Brave
543:# Linux — Google Chrome
550:# macOS — Brave
557:# macOS — Google Chrome
567:**Why `--user-data-dir`?** Without it, launching a Chromium-family browser while a regular instance is already running typically opens a new window on the existing process — and that existing process was not started with `--remote-debugging-port`, so port 9222 never opens. A dedicated user-data-dir forces a fresh browser process where the debug port actually listens. `--no-first-run --no-default-browser-check` skips the first-launch wizard for the fresh profile.
569:**Chrome 136+ makes the dedicated profile mandatory.** Two separate mechanisms are in play, and neither applies once you pass a non-default `--user-data-dir`. First, since [Chrome 136](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port) `--remote-debugging-port` and `--remote-debugging-pipe` "will no longer be respected if attempting to debug the default Chrome data directory" — the flag is silently ignored, no dialog, and `/browser connect` (or `curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`) gets connection refused even from a cold start. Second, [Chrome 144+](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp-debug-your-browser-session) adds an opt-in *approval* flow for debugging your real profile: you enable it under `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`, and Chrome then shows an **"Allow remote debugging?"** dialog for **every incoming connection** (not once per launch), with nothing listening until you press **Allow**. If you see that dialog, you are on the approval path, not the flag path. The fix is exactly the commands above: point `--user-data-dir` somewhere other than your default profile directory (e.g. `$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug`), which needs neither the toggle nor the dialog. This applies to Chrome, Chromium, Edge, and Brave builds that have picked up the change.
571:A dedicated profile starts out signed out of everything. If you want the agent to browse with your existing logins *and* no approval dialog, use [`browser.use_real_profile`](#real-profile-browsing-use-your-own-logins) instead: it snapshots your active profile into a copy and drives that, which is a non-default user-data-dir and so never triggers either mechanism.

594:If you do **not** set any cloud credentials and don't use `/browser connect`, Hermes can still use the browser tools through a local Chromium install driven by `agent-browser`.

414:##### What Hermes does
415:- Sends a deterministic profile-scoped `userId` to Camofox so the server can reuse the same Firefox profile across sessions.
417:- Scopes the `userId` to the active Hermes profile, so different Hermes profiles get different browser profiles (profile isolation).

421:- If your Camofox server build treats every request as ephemeral (e.g. always calls `browser.newContext()` without loading a stored profile), Hermes cannot make those sessions persist. Make sure you are running a Camofox build that implements userId-based profile persistence.

487:### Lightpanda local engine
508:- **Browser Use mode (the default).** Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself — one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task) — and points the Browser Use CLI at it. No Chromium, Playwright or Node.js is needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. All of these processes share one on-disk HTTP cache at `$HERMES_HOME/cache/browser-use/lightpanda/http-cache`, so repeat visits skip re-downloading assets. Hermes passes the cache flag only when the installed Lightpanda supports it (0.3.x+); older binaries simply run without a cache. To clear it, stop your Lightpanda sessions first, then delete that directory. Lightpanda has no graphical renderer, so `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable and the tool description tells the model to work text-first; it also holds one page per session, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (tracked upstream in [lightpanda-io/browser#1962](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/issues/1962)).
511:**When the engine is ignored.** `browser.engine` is the lowest-precedence browser setting: a cloud provider (including the Nous subscription browser — and on never-configured setups, any `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` / `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env` auto-selects one), Camofox, a `browser.cdp_url` / `/browser connect` override, or `browser.use_real_profile` all take precedence. 533:To start a Chromium-family browser manually with CDP enabled, use a dedicated user-data-dir so the debug port actually comes up even if the browser is already running with your normal profile:
567:**Why `--user-data-dir`?** Without it, launching a Chromium-family browser while a regular instance is already running typically opens a new window on the existing process — and that existing process was not started with `--remote-debugging-port`, so port 9222 never opens. A dedicated user-data-dir forces a fresh browser process where the debug port actually listens. `--no-first-run --no-default-browser-check` skips the first-launch wizard for the fresh profile.
569:**Chrome 136+ makes the dedicated profile mandatory.** Two separate mechanisms are in play, and neither applies once you pass a non-default `--user-data-dir`. First, since [Chrome 136](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port) `--remote-debugging-port` and `--remote-debugging-pipe` "will no longer be respected if attempting to debug the default Chrome data directory" — the flag is silently ignored, no dialog, and `/browser connect` (or `curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`) gets connection refused even from a cold start. If you see that dialog, you are on the approval path, not the flag path.
