487:### Lightpanda local engine
508:- **Browser Use mode (the default).** Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself — one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task) — and points the Browser Use CLI at it. No Chromium, Playwright or Node.js is needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. All of these processes share one on-disk HTTP cache at `$HERMES_HOME/cache/browser-use/lightpanda/http-cache`, so repeat visits skip re-downloading assets. Hermes passes the cache flag only when the installed Lightpanda supports it (0.3.x+); older binaries simply run without a cache. To clear it, stop your Lightpanda sessions first, then delete that directory. Lightpanda has no graphical renderer, so `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable and the tool description tells the model to work text-first; it also holds one page per session, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (tracked upstream in [lightpanda-io/browser#1962](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/issues/1962)).
511:**When the engine is ignored.** `browser.engine` is the lowest-precedence browser setting: a cloud provider (including the Nous subscription browser — and on never-configured setups, any `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` / `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env` auto-selects one), Camofox, a `browser.cdp_url` / `/browser connect` override, or `browser.use_real_profile` all take precedence. Picking Lightpanda in `hermes tools` writes `cloud_provider: local` for you; `/browser status` and `hermes doctor` report when the engine is configured but shadowed, and by what.
513:### Local Chromium-family browser via CDP (`/browser connect`)
533:To start a Chromium-family browser manually with CDP enabled, use a dedicated user-data-dir so the debug port actually comes up even if the browser is already running with your normal profile:
567:**Why `--user-data-dir`?** Without it, launching a Chromium-family browser while a regular instance is already running typically opens a new window on the existing process — and that existing process was not started with `--remote-debugging-port`, so port 9222 never opens. A dedicated user-data-dir forces a fresh browser process where the debug port actually listens. `--no-first-run --no-default-browser-check` skips the first-launch wizard for the fresh profile.
569:**Chrome 136+ makes the dedicated profile mandatory.** Two separate mechanisms are in play, and neither applies once you pass a non-default `--user-data-dir`. First, since [Chrome 136](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port) `--remote-debugging-port` and `--remote-debugging-pipe` "will no longer be respected if attempting to debug the default Chrome data directory" — the flag is silently ignored, no dialog, and `/browser connect` (or `curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`) gets connection refused even from a cold start. Second, [Chrome 144+](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp-debug-your-browser-session) adds an opt-in *approval* flow for debugging your real profile: you enable it under `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`, and Chrome then shows an **"Allow remote debugging?"** dialog for **every incoming connection** (not once per launch), with nothing listening until you press **Allow**. If you see that dialog, you are on the approval path, not the flag path. The fix is exactly the commands above: point `--user-data-dir` somewhere other than your default profile directory (e.g. `$HOME/.hermes/chrome-debug`), which needs neither the toggle nor the dialog. This applies to Chrome, Chromium, Edge, and Brave builds that have picked up the change.
571:A dedicated profile starts out signed out of everything. If you want the agent to browse with your existing logins *and* no approval dialog, use [`browser.use_real_profile`](#real-profile-browsing-use-your-own-logins) instead: it snapshots your active profile into a copy and drives that, which is a non-default user-data-dir and so never triggers either mechanism.

391:#### Persistent browser sessions
393:By default, each Camofox session gets a random identity — cookies and logins don't survive across agent restarts. To enable persistent browser sessions, add the following to `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
398:    managed_persistence: true
404:Hermes reads `browser.camofox.managed_persistence`, **not** a top-level `managed_persistence`. A common mistake is writing:
408:managed_persistence: true
414:##### What Hermes does
415:- Sends a deterministic profile-scoped `userId` to Camofox so the server can reuse the same Firefox profile across sessions.
417:- Scopes the `userId` to the active Hermes profile, so different Hermes profiles get different browser profiles (profile isolation).
419:##### What Hermes does not do
420:- It does not force persistence on the Camofox server. Hermes only sends a stable `userId`; the server must honor it by mapping that `userId` to a persistent Firefox profile directory.
421:- If your Camofox server build treats every request as ephemeral (e.g. always calls `browser.newContext()` without loading a stored profile), Hermes cannot make those sessions persist. Make sure you are running a Camofox build that implements userId-based profile persistence.
423:##### Verify it's working
431:If step 5 logs you out, the Camofox server isn't honoring the stable `userId`. Double-check your config path, confirm you fully restarted Hermes after editing `config.yaml`, and verify your Camofox server version supports persistent per-user profiles.
433:##### Where state lives
435:Hermes derives the stable `userId` from the profile-scoped directory `~/.hermes/browser_auth/camofox/` (or the equivalent under `$HERMES_HOME` for non-default profiles). The actual browser profile data lives on the Camofox server side, keyed by that `userId`. To fully reset a persistent profile, clear it on the Camofox server and remove the corresponding Hermes profile's state directory.
437:#### Externally managed Camofox sessions
439:When another app drives the visible Camofox browser (a desktop assistant, a custom integration, another agent), configure Hermes to operate inside that same identity instead of spawning its own isolated profile.
467:- Hermes skips destructive cleanup at task end (same as `managed_persistence: true`). The other app's tab/cookies/profile survive.
479:**Picking `session_key`:** if you want Hermes to reliably attach to a *specific* existing tab, set `session_key` to the `listItemId` the external app used when creating it. If you leave `session_key` unset and only set `user_id`, Hermes generates a per-task `session_key` (`task_<id>`) — Hermes will share cookies and the profile with the external app, but will open its own tab alongside instead of reusing one.
483:#### VNC live view
487:### Lightpanda local engine
508:- **Browser Use mode (the default).** Hermes launches `lightpanda serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port <free>` itself — one process per `browser_exec` session name (or per task) — and points the Browser Use CLI at it. No Chromium, Playwright or Node.js is needed. The process is reaped after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, on exit, and by the orphan sweep if Hermes crashes. All of these processes share one on-disk HTTP cache at `$HERMES_HOME/cache/browser-use/lightpanda/http-cache`, so repeat visits skip re-downloading assets. Hermes passes the cache flag only when the installed Lightpanda supports it (0.3.x+); older binaries simply run without a cache. To clear it, stop your Lightpanda sessions first, then delete that directory. Lightpanda has no graphical renderer, so `capture_screenshot()` is unavailable and the tool description tells the model to work text-first; it also holds one page per session, so the model is told to call `new_tab()` once and `goto_url()` afterwards (tracked upstream in [lightpanda-io/browser#1962](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/issues/1962)).
511:**When the engine is ignored.** `browser.engine` is the lowest-precedence browser setting: a cloud provider (including the Nous subscription browser — and on never-configured setups, any `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` / `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env` auto-selects one), Camofox, a `browser.cdp_url` / `/browser connect` override, or `browser.use_real_profile` all take precedence. 491:Lightpanda is a **local engine** (a browser source, like "Local Browser"), not a cloud provider. Install the binary and put it on your `PATH` (see the [Lightpanda installation guide](https://lightpanda.io/docs/run-locally/installation/one-liner)), then pick **Lightpanda** in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, or set:
905:## Limitations
911:- **No file downloads** — cannot download files from the browser
    74	Browser Use mode uses the [Browser Use CLI 3.0](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use) instead of the built-in browser tools. The agent writes and executes Python in the browser to click, type, drag, scrape, and interact with webpages.
    75	
    76	**This is the default browser mode**: when `browser.backend` is unset and the `browser-use` CLI is runnable (installed, or available through `uvx`), the agent gets the single `browser_exec` tool. If the CLI can't run, Hermes falls back to the built-in browser tools automatically.
    77	
    78	The mode is a **driver** that composes with your configured browser backend: it drives Hermes' own headless Chromium, a Nous-subscription cloud browser, Browserbase, Firecrawl, or Browser Use cloud browsers — whichever browser source is selected in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation. The one exception is Camofox, which has no CDP endpoint for the harness to attach to; Camofox setups automatically keep the built-in browser tools.
    79	
    80	**Local browsing uses the packaged Chromium, not your own Chrome.** With no cloud provider or `/browser connect` endpoint configured, Hermes launches the same Chromium that the built-in tools use (installed via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, driven through agent-browser) and points the Browser Use CLI at it. Your installed Chrome is never touched, so there is no `chrome://inspect` remote-debugging toggle to enable and no "Allow remote debugging?" popup — and it works on headless hosts with no Chrome at all. The browser is shared with the built-in stack's lifecycle: it is closed after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, at exit, and by the orphan sweep. To drive a browser you're signed in to, use `/browser connect` or the [real-profile toggle](#real-profile-browsing-use-your-own-logins).
    81	
    82	**Concurrent sessions:** `browser_exec` accepts a `session=<name>` argument that isolates browser work per name on every backend. Each name gets its own harness daemon (its own IPC socket, log, and state) and its own browser (a separate packaged Chromium locally, a separate cloud browser on cloud backends) — so parallel subagents or simultaneous chats no longer clobber a single shared connection. Omitting `session` uses the shared default daemon, which is fine for one-at-a-time browsing.
    83	
    84	To opt out and force the built-in browser tools, use `/browser use off`, or:
    85	
    86	```yaml
    87	# Add to ~/.hermes/config.yaml
    88	browser:
    89	  backend: "off"
    90	```
    91	
    92	(`backend: "browser-use"` remains valid to force the mode explicitly.)
    93	
    94	Browser Use's own cloud browsers need `browser-use auth login` or `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`; other browser sources use their existing credentials unchanged.
    95	
    96	:::note
    97	Because Browser Use mode executes model-written Python on your machine, the
    98	`browser_exec` tool is only offered to sessions that also have terminal
    99	access. Platforms configured without the terminal toolset (e.g. a locked-down
   100	messaging surface) keep the default browser tools instead.
   803	
   804	**Detection happens automatically** via a persistent CDP supervisor — one WebSocket per task that subscribes to Page/Runtime/Target events. The supervisor also populates a `frame_tree` field in the snapshot so the agent can see the iframe structure of the current page, including cross-origin (OOPIF) iframes.
   805	
   806	**Availability matrix:**
   807	
   808	| Backend | Detection via `pending_dialogs` | Response (`browser_dialog` tool) |
   809	|---|---|---|
   810	| Local Chrome via `/browser connect` or `browser.cdp_url` | ✓ | ✓ full workflow |
   811	| Browserbase | ✓ | ✓ full workflow (via injected XHR bridge) |
   812	| Camofox / default local agent-browser | ✗ | ✗ (no CDP endpoint) |
   813	
   814	**How it works on Browserbase.** Browserbase's CDP proxy auto-dismisses real native dialogs server-side within ~10ms, so we can't use `Page.handleJavaScriptDialog`. The supervisor injects a small script via `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` that overrides `window.alert`/`confirm`/`prompt` with a synchronous XHR. We intercept those XHRs via `Fetch.enable` — the page's JS thread stays blocked on the XHR until we call `Fetch.fulfillRequest` with the agent's response. `prompt()` return values round-trip back into page JS unchanged.
   815	
   816	**Dialog policy** is configured in `config.yaml` under `browser.dialog_policy`:
   817	
   818	| Policy | Behavior |
   819	|--------|----------|
   820	| `must_respond` (default) | Capture, surface in snapshot, wait for explicit `browser_dialog()` call. Safety auto-dismiss after `browser.dialog_timeout_s` (default 300s) so a buggy agent can't stall forever. |
   821	| `auto_dismiss` | Capture, dismiss immediately. Agent still sees the dialog in `browser_state` history but doesn't have to act. |
   822	| `auto_accept` | Capture, accept immediately. Useful when navigating pages with aggressive `beforeunload` prompts. |
   823	
   824	**Frame tree** inside `browser_snapshot.frame_tree` is capped to 30 frames and OOPIF depth 2 to keep payloads bounded on ad-heavy pages. A `truncated: true` flag surfaces when limits were hit; agents needing the full tree can use `browser_cdp` with `Page.getFrameTree`.
   825	
   826	## Practical Examples
   827	
   828	### Filling Out a Web Form
   829	
   830	```
   831	User: Sign up for an account on example.com with my email john@example.com
   832	
   833	Agent workflow:
   834	1. browser_navigate("https://example.com/signup")
   835	2. browser_snapshot()  → sees form fields with refs
   836	3. browser_type(ref="@e3", text="john@example.com")
   837	4. browser_type(ref="@e5", text="SecurePass123")
   838	5. browser_click(ref="@e8")  → clicks "Create Account"
   839	6. browser_snapshot()  → confirms success
   840	```
   841	
   842	### Researching Dynamic Content
   843	
   844	```
   845	User: What are the top trending repos on GitHub right now?
   846	
   847	Agent workflow:
   848	1. browser_navigate("https://github.com/trending")
   849	2. browser_snapshot(full=true)  → reads trending repo list
   850	3. Returns formatted results
   851	```
   852	
   853	## Session Recording
   854	
   855	Automatically record browser sessions as WebM video files:
   856	
   857	```yaml
   858	browser:
   859	  record_sessions: true  # default: false
   860	```
   861	
   862	When enabled, recording starts automatically on the first `browser_navigate` and saves to `~/.hermes/browser_recordings/` when the session closes. Works in both local and cloud (Browserbase) modes. Recordings older than 72 hours are automatically cleaned up.
   863	
   864	## Headed Mode (Visible Browser Window)
   865	
   866	By default, the local browser runs headless. Enable headed mode to get a visible Chromium window you can watch and interact with:
   867	
   868	```yaml
   869	browser:
   870	  headed: true  # default: false
   119	def _eval_js_secret(task_id: str, expression: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
   120	    """Evaluate a SECRET-BEARING JS expression. Supervisor CDP-WS only.
   121	
   122	    Fails closed: there is deliberately NO fallback to the agent-browser CLI
   123	    ``eval`` path, because that places the expression — and therefore the
   124	    credential bytes — in subprocess argv, visible to any process listing.
   125	    When no supervisor session is available the caller gets a typed refusal
   126	    (``error_type='supervisor_required'``) and nothing is written.
   127	    """
   128	    try:
   129	        supervisor = _ensure_supervisor(task_id)
   130	    except Exception as exc:
   131	        logger.debug("vault fill: supervisor unavailable (%s)", exc)
   132	        supervisor = None
   133	
   134	    if supervisor is None:
   135	        return {
   136	            "success": False,
   137	            "error_type": "supervisor_required",
   138	            "error": (
   139	                "Vault fill requires the supervised browser session (direct "
   140	                "CDP WebSocket). The fallback eval path would place the "
   141	                "credential in subprocess argv, so it is never used for "
   142	                "secrets. Start the browser through the Hermes-managed "
   143	                "session and retry."
   144	            ),
   145	        }
   146

content.text:
**Hermes already supports browsers inside our own VM. The simplest candidate is managed Chromium with its default Browser Use driver.** Findings are from pinned commit `f97608f`; no browsers were installed or run.

| Ready-made option | What runs in our VM | Setup / practical limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Managed Chromium + Browser Use driver** | Hermes launches packaged Chromium through `agent-browser`; `browser_exec` runs Python browser helpers against its local CDP endpoint. | Select `cloud_provider: local`; leave the driver default or select `backend: browser-use`. Requires Chromium, `agent-browser`, Browser Use CLI, and terminal capability. Supports screenshots, DOM operations and raw CDP. [Driver selection](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_use_cli.py:219), [local Chromium connection](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_use_cli.py:403). |
| **Managed Chromium + built-in tools** | Same local Chromium; explicit `browser_navigate`, snapshot, click/type, eval, vision, etc. | `backend: "off"` selects these tools. Requires `agent-browser` plus Chromium. Useful if we prefer a more structured agent tool surface. [Selection and prerequisites](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_tool_install.py:296). |
| **Camofox** | Self-hosted Node server wrapping Firefox-based Camoufox; Hermes uses its REST API. | Run its server/container and configure `CAMOFOX_URL`. Uses built-in tools, **not** the Browser Use driver because it lacks CDP. Managed persistence requires server support and preserved server storage. 1 # clanker v1 scope and build approach 2 3 ## State 4 5 **clanker v1 is a hosted Hermes-based Slack assistant for general browser tasks and access management. Reuse Hermes first; focus clanker-specific work on routing and authorization, and add code only for demonstrated gaps.** 6 7 The repository contains this scope, a verification strategy and source review, plus a pinned stock Hermes local baseline and clanker Slack setup files. The local CLI starts, 47 targeted upstream routing/session tests pass, and real Slack owner commands work in a DM and the test channel; see [LOCAL_BASELINE.md](verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md). The full Slack/browser E2E, deployed reviewer experience, and v1 acceptance remain open. Upstream documentation and synthetic tests establish narrower capabilities, not that our chosen deployment has passed its requirements. 8 9 The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification. There is no requirement to build a new agent harness, Slack connector, browser engine, vault, or TOTP algorithm. 10 11 Slack is the v1 interface. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Sahan and Nishank enter through the demo workspace invitation/entry link and use clanker without local setup or their own model-provider accounts. Inference is owner-funded. 12 13 The assignment's core is browser tasks and secure access management. Private DMs, shared channel context, and protection between reviewers are additional v1 behavior requested by the user. A general self-service SaaS platform is not a prerequisite. 14 15 ### Preferred inference setup: owner's ChatGPT account 16 17 Prefer using the owner's existing ChatGPT subscription through Hermes's ChatGPT/Codex OAuth provider for the cloud baseline, to avoid purchasing separate API credits for eligible model usage. Reviewers still use Slack without their own model-provider accounts. This is the preferred setup to evaluate, not a verified funding arrangement. 18 19 [Hermes documents](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers) device-code authorization, which lets the owner approve login in their browser while Hermes runs and stores its authentication on the cloud host. [OpenAI documents](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites) eligible plan usage in supported integrations; Hermes's exact account eligibility and quota accounting remain unverified for this deployment. Before relying on this route, establish that the intended owner-funded reviewer usage is supported, run a small inference request, and inspect the resulting usage and billing. Verify authentication refresh and persistence across a cloud restart with the owner's laptop out of the execution path. 20 21 Subscription-funded inference does not establish coverage for hosting or separately billed browser/tool services. Record those costs separately. Any alternative paid inference setup remains a separate decision if the preferred route cannot meet the requirements. 22 23 ## Reuse from Hermes 24 25 Pin the Hermes version and required integrations, configure them, and verify their behavior in the deployed Slack experience. 26 27 | Capability | Starting point | What clanker must establish | 28 | --- | --- | --- | 29 | Agent harness | Hermes's agent loop, tools, skills, and session machinery | General tasks work with the selected model and enabled tools. | 30 | Slack interface | Hermes's existing Slack adapter and gateway | App configuration, authenticated admission, correct conversation routing, and replies. | 31 | Browser automation | Existing Browser Use integration and supported browser backends | Background browser work, file workflows, independent sessions, and saved-access reuse. | 32 | Credentials and 2FA | Hermes's credential vault, protected browser filling, TOTP support, and access-management controls | Reviewers can securely provide, reuse, and remove access through the hosted experience. Resolve the TOTP choice below. | 33 | Profiles and conversations | Existing profile routing, DM/channel/thread sessions, memory, and persistence | The selected configuration enforces the intended tenant, owner, and audience boundaries across turns and restarts. | 34 35 Start from the documented [browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/), [profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), and [session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions). Native vault documentation shows interactive CLI/Desktop flows; a complete secure Slack collection and revocation flow still needs validation. Treat that as a check, not proof that a new credential service is required. 36 37 ## Architecture and routing contract 38 39 **Start by evaluating one shared Hermes deployment serving separate conversations and profiles.** Neither a permanent instance per user nor an instance per tenant is required by this scope. Profiles and sessions organize state; the deployment and tool configuration must enforce the required access boundaries. Introduce additional processes or sandboxes where the chosen tools require them, based on evidence. 40 41 ```mermaid 42 flowchart TD 43 Slack["Slack workspaces
Private DMs and shared channels/threads"] <--> Gateway["Hermes Slack gateway"] 44 Gateway <--> Routing["Tenant, sender, context, and access routing
Use existing configuration first"] 45 Routing <--> Private["Private conversations
Owner-scoped history and resources"] 46 Routing <--> Shared["Shared conversations
Context scoped to channel audience"] 47 Private <--> Tools["Existing Hermes tools
Authorized browser, vault, and file access"] 48 Shared <-->|Only resources authorized for this shared turn| Tools 49 ``` 50 51 These boxes describe responsibilities, not mandatory new services. The routing checks may be Hermes configuration, supported extension points, or a small clanker integration. A separate custom gateway, authorization service, provisioner, or broker must earn its place by fixing a demonstrated gap. Run Hermes in its upstream runtime; TypeScript remains the preference for clanker-owned integration code where appropriate. 52 53 | Routing decision | Required behavior | 54 | --- | --- | 55 | Tenant | Derive workspace/installation identity from authenticated Slack events. Include it in user, conversation, and resource routing. Reject unknown or unauthorized requesters instead of falling into a privileged default. | 56 | Conversation and audience | A 1:1 DM loads that user's private context. A channel/thread loads context authorized for that channel's audience. Workspace membership alone does not reveal private-channel history. | 57 | Requester and resource owner | Keep the sender, account/resource owner, and conversation audience distinct. Validate ownership before using credentials, browsers, files, history, or controls. Another participant's follow-up conveys no authority over someone else's private work. | 58 | Context and tools | Scope memory, session recall, learned skills, files, artifacts, browser state, and credentials to the current authorized context. Prompt instructions and model-supplied owner IDs cannot grant access. | 59 | Result destination | Return private account results privately. Sharing requires the owner's approval of the specific content and audience. Shared output grants no access to its source account or private files. | 60 61 Session separation and profile routing are useful controls, but must be tested together with tools and persistence. Shared-profile memory or session recall must not expose DM content in a channel. Model-generated code must not have unrestricted access to other owners' files, the shared history store, or platform administrator credentials. Use supported scoped tools and isolated execution where needed; disable or adapt a tool whose access cannot be constrained. 62 63 Keep retained history, recovery state, browser access, and artifacts durable across restarts, with their owner/audience associations intact. Use existing persistence when it meets these needs. Hosting, storage, and the exact profile/session mapping remain implementation choices; no particular cloud vendor, database, or object store is mandated. 64 65 For v1 delivery, the reviewers use one demo workspace. Routing must still carry tenant identity and be checked against another tenant identity without requiring a public onboarding or provisioning product. 66 67 ### Example: collaboration involving a private account 68 69 Sahan and Nishank discuss a report in a shared thread. Both contributions belong to that thread's context. If the work needs Sahan's private account, route that part into an owner-authorized private conversation/run, using existing capabilities where possible. Obtain missing authorization through his DM or secure handoff. Private observations never enter the shared conversation automatically. Sahan receives the result privately and may approve selected content for publication back into the thread. Nishank can continue the shared discussion without gaining authority over Sahan's account. 70 71 ## Required behavior 72 73 1. **Perform general browser and file tasks.** Accept natural-language goals across different, unfamiliar websites. Discover and upload an intended existing file; support download, inspection/transformation, and upload when requested. Site-specific scripts are not evidence of general capability. 74 2. **Collect, reuse, and revoke access.** Support secure input or login handoff for passwords, API keys, OAuth/browser access, and card details when needed. Keep secrets out of chat and model inputs. Reuse encrypted saved access and browser sessions across tasks and fresh browser runs. Owners can remove access; affected active work and saved sessions must not silently retain the revoked authority. 75 3. **Preserve private and shared boundaries.** DMs, personal memory, credentials, browser state, and private files stay owner-scoped. Channel discussions and intentionally shared material stay audience-scoped. Concurrent users cannot take over each other's sessions, account access, private history, approvals, or artifacts. 76 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, provide useful brief progress, clarify material details, and offer private human handoff when needed. Persist the task through expired access, failures, and restarts; resume without blindly replaying completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 77 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain owner confirmation for concrete consequential actions such as purchases, external messages, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Confirm the actual website state or artifact before reporting completion. Approval for an action and approval to share its private result are separate permissions. 78 79 ### TOTP: existing capability, unresolved product choice 80 81 Reuse Hermes's existing TOTP implementation if automatic generation is included. The user's preferred flow is to supply the current code through secure input or a private browser handoff, keeping the setup key with the user. 82 83 The original assignment explicitly requires accepting a TOTP setup key once and generating subsequent codes. **Manual code entry alone does not satisfy that criterion.** Resolve whether to demonstrate native automatic TOTP with the user's agreement or obtain an accepted assignment exception before declaring v1 complete. Automatic generation as an opt-in was discussed as a possibility, not settled. This choice does not require implementing a new TOTP algorithm and does not block the initial Slack/browser/routing proof. 84 85 ## Now: build in this order 86 87 1. **Configure a runnable Hermes baseline.** Pin versions, enable Slack and the existing browser/vault capabilities, and provide reproducible setup and secret-free environment examples. Identify the simplest suitable hosting and persistence arrangement. 88 2. **Configure the intended routes.** Map verified workspace and sender identities to private DM or shared channel context and the correct resources. Use existing profiles, sessions, and admission controls first. Record the mappings and verify a two-user example before adding custom services. 89 3. **Exercise the complete reviewer flow.** From Slack, request browser work, provide access securely, reuse it, complete the file workflow, handle a failure, and remove access. Check shared collaboration and private boundaries using the actual enabled tools. Record passes, failures, and untested behavior. 90 4. **Fix demonstrated gaps only.** Prefer configuration, then supported plugins/extensions, then small integration changes. Potential gaps include secure Slack input, owner-bound resource selection, or controlled result delivery; none is presumed to need custom code before the baseline is tested. Keep passing upstream features intact. 91 5. **Validate the hosted experience and package the result.** Repeat the acceptance checks with the developer's laptop out of the execution path. Produce the repository, entry link, demo, and access-management note. Attribute Hermes and other reused components accurately. 92 93 **Done when:** the required behavior works through the deployed reviewer experience, the four deliverables exist, and the release evidence passes. Code volume and the number of custom components are not completion criteria. Record unsupported or unresolved requirements explicitly; do not mark v1 complete while they remain unmet. 94 95 ## Release evidence 96 97 | Area | Evidence required | 98 | --- | --- | 99 | Inference authentication and funding | Verify the chosen ChatGPT/Codex OAuth route supports the owner's account and intended hosted reviewer use. Record observed model-usage accounting and any separate charges. Exercise authentication refresh and restart persistence without depending on the owner's laptop. If this route is unavailable, record the unmet setup choice and agree an alternative before relying on it. | 100 | General browser and file work | Complete real tasks on at least two different websites through the same engine. Verify destination state independently of the agent's completion message. Find and upload the intended existing file, and complete download/inspection or transformation/upload. Treat two websites as an initial proof, not universal coverage. | 101 | Access lifecycle | A reviewer securely connects and removes access through the hosted experience. Verify saved-credential reuse in a fresh browser, test saved-session reuse separately, and show revocation prevents further affected access. Resolve and verify the TOTP criterion above. | 102 | Recovery and durability | Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, supply the required input, and resume the original task. Restart the runtime and retain the correct history and artifacts. Verify recovery does not duplicate a completed consequential action. | 103 | Routing, privacy, and collaboration | Two reviewers contribute to a shared task and retain its authorized context after restart. Test simultaneous private work, forged owner/tenant references, cross-user files/history/memory/skills, another participant's follow-up, and copied controls. Check that routing, enabled tools, and persisted data uphold the boundary, including another tenant identity. Demonstrate an approved result shared to a channel while private source data remains protected. | 104 | Approvals and honest completion | Another participant cannot approve the owner's private action; changed action details or sharing audiences cannot reuse an old approval. Record actual outcomes, human intervention, failures, relevant versions, and known limits. Distinguish configured, verified, unsupported, and untested capabilities. | 105 106 ## Four deliverables 107 108 | Deliverable | Completion criteria | 109 | --- | --- | 110 | Runnable repository | Pinned dependencies/upstream versions, configuration, setup instructions, secret-free environment examples, and exercised verification instructions. Include integration code only where needed. | 111 | Deployed reviewer experience | Slack invitation/entry link and hosted execution available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can use it without local setup or their own model-provider account. | 112 | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion. Include reuse/recovery where practical; inspect the exported video for exposed secrets before sharing. | 113 | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain the chosen routing/profile/session boundaries, storage, access collection/reuse/revocation, TOTP decision, recovery, and verified limits. Identify upstream functionality versus clanker changes and explicitly disclose deferred operator/provider privacy controls. | 114 115 ## Later 116 117 Self-service multi-tenant onboarding/provisioning, additional messaging interfaces, delegated account access, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and configurable approval-policy UX are outside v1. Basic shared channel context, private DMs, ordinary owner confirmations, and approved result sharing remain in v1. 118 119 Operator-access and model-provider-access privacy controls, including broader auditing, retention, training-use, and data-lifecycle controls, are deferred to clanker v2 or later as requested. This does not defer credential secrecy, protection between users/tenants, or honest disclosure of the deployed system's limits. 120 121 ## Next 122 123 Configure Hermes with Slack and its existing browser/access capabilities, then prove the two-user DM/channel routing behavior and first complete browser task. Use those results to decide what clanker code is actually necessary. Settle the remaining TOTP choice before final acceptance. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders.

**Pinned Hermes already implements “save a TOTP setup key once, generate future codes.” Clanker’s secure Slack collection and full acceptance remain unfinished.**

1. **Setup-key collection exists in CLI/desktop plumbing.** CLI uses hidden input for a base32 setup key or `otpauth://` URI, then saves it with the login. Normalization accepts TOTP, including nondefault digits/period/algorithm; HOTP is rejected. [CLI input](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/vault.py:73), [normalization](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:74). Desktop/TUI `vault.add` accepts the secret payload directly and returns only its ID. [API](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/methods_vault.py:135).

2. **The seed is encrypted in the owner/profile vault.** `otp_secret` enters the encrypted login payload; Fernet encrypts the vault file with mode `0600`. Both encrypted vault and decryption key live under that profile’s `HERMES_HOME/vault`, so encryption does not replace runtime/storage isolation. [Seed storage](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:342), [encryption](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:296), [paths](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:194).

3. **Automatic generation and direct browser filling exist.** `resolve_otp(handle)` decrypts the stored seed and calls the RFC 6238 implementation. `browser_vault_enter_code` obtains that code server-side, registers redaction, sends it through the secret CDP fill path, and returns success/count/origin/source metadata rather than the code. [Generator](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:106), [backend](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_backends/local.py:32), [fill](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_vault_tool.py:335). A pre-saved seed therefore avoids an interactive code prompt.

4. **Slack enrollment is the integration gap.** Targeted searches found prompt registration in the TUI bridge, none in the Slack adapter/gateway paths. Missing callbacks return `prompt_unavailable`. Also, the existing browser “save login” tool currently stores **identifier/password only**, omitting a setup seed even if a custom prompt returned one. We need a secure owner-bound handoff that writes the seed through the vault API; pasting it into Slack is not that flow. [Missing-prompt guard](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_vault_tool.py:304), [save payload](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_vault_tool.py:318).

Its `expected_origin` check only guards against the page changing during that fill. Password fill separately validates `meta.allowed_origins`; code entry does not. This is a **source finding, not a live reproduction**. **Reuse the vault implementation; build the hosted secure-input and task-resumption bridge.**

- **Yes, a trusted helper can save both secrets outside the model.** Call `VaultStore.add_item(kind="login", …, secret={identifier_type, identifier, password, otp_secret}, origin=…)` in the server-selected owner profile; return only `meta.id`. The method validates/normalizes the seed, writes under a lock, and returns metadata. [Implementation](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_store.py:304). Existing `vault.add` is a useful precedent: it returns `{id}` and scrubs secret-bearing errors. [Precedent](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/methods_vault.py:135).
- **The current browser prompt is synchronous.** `browser_vault_save_login` directly calls `answer = prompt(origin, host)` and proceeds immediately with that answer. Its write includes password/identifier **but not `otp_secret`**, so merely attaching a new web form callback would lose the seed. [Call and payload](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tools/browser_vault_tool.py:304). TUI’s callback synchronously waits through `_ask(..., timeout=180)`. [TUI bridge](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/agent_callbacks.py:222).
- **For VM-backed tasks, make waiting an external durable state.** Proposed flow: persist `waiting_for_input` and an owner/task/site-bound request → send the secure-page link → accepted form submission calls the trusted vault helper → persist the returned handle → requeue/resume the original task with “access available” metadata. Resume through existing `browser_vault_fill`/`browser_vault_enter_code`; never put form secrets into the conversation or task queue payload.
- **Keep scope selection and authorization in Clanker.** An opaque handle is not permission. The helper must select the authorized profile from the authenticated request, reject expired/replayed input requests, and prevent client-selected filesystem/profile paths. Existing `can_prompt_here()` also rejects unattended/single-query contexts and requires an unlock callback, confirming that the CLI/TUI callback mechanism is not already an asynchronous hosted form workflow. [Prompt gate](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/agent/vault_backends/unlock.py:162).

1	"""Credential-vault JSON-RPC handlers — the Desktop's door to the local vault.
     2	
     3	The Desktop's Settings → Credential Vault panel manages the encrypted,
     4	model-blind vault (``agent/vault_store.py``) over the same localhost WS
     5	JSON-RPC channel every other Settings surface uses. Contracts:
     6	
     7	- ``vault.list``   → metadata only ({id, kind, label, origin, created_at,
     8	  and for logins identifier/identifier_type — identifiers are visible
     9	  metadata by design}); passwords NEVER appear in any response.
    10	- ``vault.add``    → validates via ``VaultStore.add_item``; the secret
    11	  payload arrives over the local RPC channel, goes straight into the
    12	  encrypted store, and is never logged. Error strings are defensively
    13	  scrubbed with ``scrub_secret_from_text`` before they leave the handler.
    14	- ``vault.remove`` → {removed: bool}.
    15	- ``vault.sources`` / ``vault.source.set`` → external password-manager status and enable toggle.
    16	- ``vault.unlock`` / ``vault.lock`` → per-session unlock of a manager from Settings; the master
    17	  password is consumed by the manager CLI through its non-interactive channel and never stored
    18	  or logged.
    19	
    20	Every handler honours ``params.profile`` (app-global remote mode serves several profiles from one
    21	backend): the requested profile's HERMES_HOME and secret scope are bound around the body, so the
    22	vault file, manager config and manager tokens all resolve to that profile.
    23	
    24	Handlers are rebound onto server.py's globals at install time (see
    25	method_ctx.py) and may reference server module globals (``_ok``, ``_err``).
    26	"""
    27	
    28	from .method_ctx import HandlerRegistry
    29	
    30	_registry = HandlerRegistry()
    31	method = _registry.method
    32	# server.py's ``@_profile_scoped`` (applied at install): the one scoping path every RPC uses, so the
    33	# launch profile (no ``params.profile``) keeps its secret scope bound once the process multiplexes
    34	# instead of its manager-token reads raising ``UnscopedSecretError``.
    35	_profile_scoped = _registry.profile_scoped
    36	
    37	# JSON-RPC error code 5095 = vault failure (validation + store errors).
    38	# Kept as a literal inside handler bodies: handlers are rebound onto
    39	# server.py's globals, so module-level constants are not reachable there.
    40	
    41	
    42	@method("vault.list")
    43	@_profile_scoped
    44	def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    45	    """Metadata-only listing across every enabled backend (local + unlocked password managers).
    46	    Each item carries ``backend``; locked managers contribute nothing (see vault.sources)."""

**Hermes ships reusable vault UI and a hostable server, but I did not find a ready-made, credential-only web page with Clanker’s Slack-user authorization.**

- **Vault UI exists in Desktop.** Its React `VaultSettings` component collects login/password and optional `otp_secret`, calls `vault.add`, and supports removal. It depends on Desktop connection/profile state and gateway helpers, so it is reusable source rather than a standalone deployable form. [Fields](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/apps/desktop/src/app/settings/vault-settings.tsx:112), [submit](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/apps/desktop/src/app/settings/vault-settings.tsx:318).
- **A hostable server exists.** `hermes dashboard` serves the admin web UI; `hermes serve` runs the same backend without that UI. Public binding requires configured password/OAuth authentication. The server exposes JSON-RPC over `/api/ws`, including the vault methods. [Server modes](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/subcommands/dashboard.py:1), [public auth requirement](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/subcommands/dashboard.py:19), [WebSocket route](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/web_routers/chat_ws.py:583).
- **The separate web dashboard lacks a vault page in this checkout.** Searches of `web/src` found no vault form/calls; its registered pages are broad administration surfaces such as profiles, environment variables, files, sessions and system settings. The real vault form is under `apps/desktop`. [Dashboard pages](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/web/src/App.tsx:79).
- **Hosting it does not establish Clanker’s owner boundary.** Vault handlers accept `params.profile`; `_profile_scoped` selects that profile’s home from the request. The inspected vault method/dispatch path does not compare that requested profile with the authenticated user. WebSocket authentication exists, but Slack-owner-to-profile authorization is not supplied by these vault handlers. [Vault contract](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/methods_vault.py:20), [profile selection](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/server.py:551).

**Minimal reuse:** adapt the existing vault form and retain Hermes’s vault storage/fill APIs; add the narrow hosted entry page, authenticated owner/task binding, and durable resume notification. No need to build another vault engine.

# clanker v1 scope and build approach ## State **clanker v1 is a hosted Hermes-based Slack assistant for general browser tasks and access management. Reuse Hermes first; focus clanker-specific work on routing and authorization, and add code only for demonstrated gaps.** The repository contains this scope, a verification strategy and source review, plus a pinned stock Hermes local baseline and clanker Slack setup files. The local CLI starts, 47 targeted upstream routing/session tests pass, and real Slack owner commands work in a DM and the test channel; see [LOCAL_BASELINE.md](verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md). The full Slack/browser E2E, deployed reviewer experience, and v1 acceptance remain open. Upstream documentation and synthetic tests establish narrower capabilities, not that our chosen deployment has passed its requirements. **Selected browser architecture:** each assigned worker VM runs Hermes and local Chromium, controlled through Hermes's existing Browser Use driver. This is the selected v1 design; the VM pool, browser workflow, and persistence across VM replacement still require implementation and verification. The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification. There is no requirement to build a new agent harness, Slack connector, browser engine, vault, or TOTP algorithm. Slack is the v1 interface. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Sahan and Nishank enter through the demo workspace invitation/entry link and use clanker without local setup or their own model-provider accounts. Inference is owner-funded. The assignment's core is browser tasks and secure access management. Private DMs, shared channel context, and protection between reviewers are additional v1 behavior requested by the user. A general self-service SaaS platform is not a prerequisite. ### Preferred inference setup: owner's ChatGPT account Prefer using the owner's existing ChatGPT subscription through Hermes's ChatGPT/Codex OAuth provider for the cloud baseline, to avoid purchasing separate API credits for eligible model usage. Reviewers still use Slack without their own model-provider accounts. This is the preferred setup to evaluate, not a verified funding arrangement. [Hermes documents](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers) device-code authorization, which lets the owner approve login in their browser while Hermes runs and stores its authentication on the cloud host. [OpenAI documents](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites) eligible plan usage in supported integrations; Hermes's exact account eligibility and quota accounting remain unverified for this deployment. Before relying on this route, establish that the intended owner-funded reviewer usage is supported, run a small inference request, and inspect the resulting usage and billing. Verify authentication refresh and persistence across a cloud restart with the owner's laptop out of the execution path. Subscription-funded inference does not establish coverage for hosting or separately billed browser/tool services. Record those costs separately. Any alternative paid inference setup remains a separate decision if the preferred route cannot meet the requirements. ## Reuse from Hermes Pin the Hermes version and required integrations, configure them, and verify their behavior in the deployed Slack experience. | Capability | Starting point | What clanker must establish | | --- | --- | --- | | Agent harness | Hermes's agent loop, tools, skills, and session machinery | General tasks work with the selected model and enabled tools. | | Slack interface | Hermes's existing Slack adapter and gateway | App configuration, authenticated admission, correct conversation routing, and replies. | | Browser automation | Local Chromium inside the assigned worker VM, controlled by Hermes's existing Browser Use driver (`browser_exec`) | Background browser work, uploads/downloads, secure login/handoff, scoped browser persistence, and saved-access reuse across worker replacement. | | Credentials and 2FA | Hermes's credential vault, protected browser filling, TOTP support, and access-management controls | Reviewers can securely provide, reuse, and remove access through the hosted experience. Resolve the TOTP choice below. | | Profiles and conversations | Existing profile routing, DM/channel/thread sessions, memory, and persistence | The selected configuration enforces the intended tenant, owner, and audience boundaries across turns and restarts. | Start from the documented [browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/), [profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), and [session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions). Native vault documentation shows interactive CLI/Desktop flows; a complete secure Slack collection and revocation flow still needs validation. Treat that as a check, not proof that a new credential service is required. ## Architecture and routing contract **Use a shared Slack gateway and a pool of isolated Hermes worker VMs.** The gateway binds authenticated tenant, sender, and conversation audience to an authorized profile before queueing the task. The scheduler assigns a ready VM to that private or shared context; the VM pool manager maintains clean warm spares, adds capacity within limits, and removes excess idle capacity. Each worker runs Hermes, its Browser Use driver, and local Chromium inside the same VM. Profiles and permitted browser/file state persist beyond the worker's lifetime. The hosting provider, pool sizes, idle timeout, and storage implementation remain open choices. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["Slack workspaces
Private DMs and shared channels/threads"] <--> Gateway["Hermes Slack gateway"] Gateway --> Routing["Authenticated tenant, sender, and audience
Bind authorized profile and task"] Routing --> Queue["Durable task queue + scheduler
Fair dispatch, leases, bounded retries"] Queue -->|Assign task| Worker["Assigned worker VM
Hermes + Browser Use driver + local Chromium
One authorized private or shared context"] Queue -->|Pending demand| Pool["VM pool manager / autoscaler
Ready-spare target, VM limits, idle timeout"] Pool -->|Lifecycle calls| Provider["VM provider API"] Provider -->|Provision or stop| Worker Worker -->|Capacity and health| Pool Worker <--> Access["Enforced resource access
Only the current context's authorized state"] Access <--> State["Durable profile home, browser state, and files
Separate task and delivery records"] Worker -->|Persist result| Delivery["Result delivery + owner-bound approval enforcement"] Delivery --> Gateway ``` These boxes describe responsibilities, not mandatory separate services. Reuse Hermes's Slack adapter, agent runtime, browser driver, vault, and session machinery. Routing checks may use existing configuration, supported extension points, or a small clanker integration. The scheduler and VM pool manager can share a backend service. The remote worker-to-gateway handoff must bind and durably record results before releasing a worker; reuse existing Slack delivery where it fits. Run Hermes in its upstream runtime; TypeScript remains the preference for clanker-owned integration code where appropriate. ### Selected browser stack: local Chromium + Browser Use Use the existing [Browser Use driver](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/#browser-use-mode-default) with local Chromium. Hermes remains the agent making decisions; Browser Use supplies browser control through `browser_exec`. A hosted browser service is not part of the selected v1 baseline. Make local selection explicit instead of relying on credential autodetection: ```yaml browser: cloud_provider: local backend: browser-use ``` Build the worker image with pinned, compatible versions of Hermes, the Browser Use CLI, `agent-browser`, Chromium, and the required Linux dependencies. The pinned Hermes release installs/discovers the Browser Use CLI separately; pinning Hermes alone does not pin that driver. Complete installation during image construction so assigned tasks do not depend on first-use downloads. Keep **Hermes itself, the Python executed by `browser_exec`, and Chromium inside the assigned VM**. Running only the browser there would leave driver code executing on the shared host. Expose only the current context's authorized profile, browser state, and files; a shared channel worker must not receive a participant's private account state. Persist the entire authorized `HERMES_HOME`, including `state.db` conversation and tool history, plus the dedicated browser profile and required workspace files/artifacts. Clanker's task record references the Hermes profile and session rather than duplicating chat history. Default local Chromium sessions are temporary, so configure and verify a persistent browser profile; a dedicated local Chromium instance connected through CDP is an existing integration option. The exact persistence mechanism remains to be validated. Restoring conversation history and cookies does not by itself restore a live page, unfinished form, or in-flight action. Before accepting this stack, exercise secure credential filling and human login/handoff, saved-login reuse in a fresh browser, saved-session reuse separately, download/inspection or transformation/upload, owner/audience separation, revocation, and recovery after worker replacement. These are pending acceptance checks, not capabilities already verified in clanker's local baseline. | Routing decision | Required behavior | | --- | --- | | Tenant | Derive workspace/installation identity from authenticated Slack events. Include it in user, conversation, and resource routing. Reject unknown or unauthorized requesters instead of falling into a privileged default. | | Conversation and audience | A 1:1 DM loads that user's private context. A channel/thread loads context authorized for that channel's audience. Workspace membership alone does not reveal private-channel history. | | Requester and resource owner | Keep the sender, account/resource owner, and conversation audience distinct. Validate ownership before using credentials, browsers, files, history, or controls. Another participant's follow-up conveys no authority over someone else's private work. | | Context and tools | Scope memory, session recall, learned skills, files, artifacts, browser state, and credentials to the current authorized context. Prompt instructions and model-supplied owner IDs cannot grant access. | | Result destination | Return private account results privately. Sharing requires the owner's approval of the specific content and audience. Shared output grants no access to its source account or private files. | Session separation and profile routing are useful controls, but must be tested together with tools and persistence. Shared-profile memory or session recall must not expose DM content in a channel. Model-generated code must not have unrestricted access to other owners' files, the shared history store, or platform administrator credentials. Use supported scoped tools and isolated execution where needed; disable or adapt a tool whose access cannot be constrained. Keep retained history, recovery state, browser access, and artifacts durable across restarts, with their owner/audience associations intact. Use existing persistence when it meets these needs. The VM execution boundary and local browser stack above are selected; the cloud vendor, storage technology, and exact profile/session mapping remain implementation choices. For v1 delivery, the reviewers use one demo workspace. Routing must still carry tenant identity and be checked against another tenant identity without requiring a public onboarding or provisioning product. ### Example: collaboration involving a private account Sahan and Nishank discuss a report in a shared thread. Both contributions belong to that thread's context. If the work needs Sahan's private account, route that part into an owner-authorized private conversation/run, using existing capabilities where possible. Obtain missing authorization through his DM or secure handoff. Private observations never enter the shared conversation automatically. Sahan receives the result privately and may approve selected content for publication back into the thread. Nishank can continue the shared discussion without gaining authority over Sahan's account. ## Required behavior 1. **Perform general browser and file tasks.** Accept natural-language goals across different, unfamiliar websites. Discover and upload an intended existing file; support download, inspection/transformation, and upload when requested. Site-specific scripts are not evidence of general capability. 2. **Collect, reuse, and revoke access.** Support secure input or login handoff for passwords, API keys, OAuth/browser access, and card details when needed. Keep secrets out of chat and model inputs. Reuse encrypted saved access and browser sessions across tasks and fresh browser runs. Owners can remove access; affected active work and saved sessions must not silently retain the revoked authority. 3. **Preserve private and shared boundaries.** DMs, personal memory, credentials, browser state, and private files stay owner-scoped. Channel discussions and intentionally shared material stay audience-scoped. Concurrent users cannot take over each other's sessions, account access, private history, approvals, or artifacts. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, provide useful brief progress, clarify material details, and offer private human handoff when needed. Persist the task through expired access, failures, and restarts; resume without blindly replaying completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain owner confirmation for concrete consequential actions such as purchases, external messages, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Confirm the actual website state or artifact before reporting completion. Approval for an action and approval to share its private result are separate permissions. ### TOTP: existing capability, unresolved product choice Reuse Hermes's existing TOTP implementation if automatic generation is included. The user's preferred flow is to supply the current code through secure input or a private browser handoff, keeping the setup key with the user. The original assignment explicitly requires accepting a TOTP setup key once and generating subsequent codes. **Manual code entry alone does not satisfy that criterion.** Resolve whether to demonstrate native automatic TOTP with the user's agreement or obtain an accepted assignment exception before declaring v1 complete. Automatic generation as an opt-in was discussed as a possibility, not settled. This choice does not require implementing a new TOTP algorithm and does not block the initial Slack/browser/routing proof. ## Now: build in this order 1. **Configure the selected local browser worker.** Pin Hermes and its browser dependencies, prepare a worker VM image with local Chromium and the Browser Use driver, enable the existing browser/vault capabilities, and provide reproducible setup and secret-free environment examples. Verify the chosen profile, browser, and workspace persistence arrangement. 2. **Configure the intended routes.** Map verified workspace and sender identities to private DM or shared channel context and the correct resources. Use existing profiles, sessions, and admission controls first. Record the mappings and verify a two-user example before adding custom services. 3. **Exercise the complete reviewer flow.** From Slack, request browser work, provide access securely, reuse it, complete the file workflow, handle a failure, and remove access. Check shared collaboration and private boundaries using the actual enabled tools. Record passes, failures, and untested behavior. 4. **Fix demonstrated gaps only.** Prefer configuration, then supported plugins/extensions, then small integration changes. Potential gaps include secure Slack input, owner-bound resource selection, or controlled result delivery; none is presumed to need custom code before the baseline is tested. Keep passing upstream features intact. 5. **Validate the hosted experience and package the result.** Repeat the acceptance checks with the developer's laptop out of the execution path. Produce the repository, entry link, demo, and access-management note. Attribute Hermes and other reused components accurately. **Done when:** the required behavior works through the deployed reviewer experience, the four deliverables exist, and the release evidence passes. Code volume and the number of custom components are not completion criteria. Record unsupported or unresolved requirements explicitly; do not mark v1 complete while they remain unmet. ## Release evidence | Area | Evidence required | | --- | --- | | Inference authentication and funding | Verify the chosen ChatGPT/Codex OAuth route supports the owner's account and intended hosted reviewer use. Record observed model-usage accounting and any separate charges. Exercise authentication refresh and restart persistence without depending on the owner's laptop. If this route is unavailable, record the unmet setup choice and agree an alternative before relying on it. | | General browser and file work | Complete real tasks on at least two different websites using the selected local Chromium + Browser Use stack inside the worker VM. Record driver/browser versions and confirm execution uses the local browser. Verify destination state independently of the agent's completion message. Find and upload the intended existing file, and complete download/inspection or transformation/upload. Treat two websites as an initial proof, not universal coverage. | | Access lifecycle | A reviewer securely connects and removes access through the hosted experience. Verify saved-credential reuse in a fresh browser, test saved-session reuse separately, and show revocation prevents further affected access. Resolve and verify the TOTP criterion above. | | Recovery and durability | Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, supply the required input, and resume the original task. This is the selected v1 design; the VM pool, browser workflow, and persistence across VM replacement still require implementation and verification. The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification.
